notes.front: What is an App Service plan?
notes.back: The set of compute resources a web app runs on; every App Service app runs in one.
notes.explanation: Whatever apps you put into the plan run on those compute resources.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure App Service plans?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: An *Azure App Service plan* defines a set of compute resources for a web app to run. An app service always runs in an App Service plan.
notes.example: Like renting a group of servers that all the web apps you place on them share.

notes.front: What is App Service automatic scaling?
notes.back: A scale-out option in which App Service makes the scaling decisions for your web apps and plan itself, based on web traffic.
notes.explanation: You don't write rules or schedules for it, unlike Azure autoscale.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Automatic scaling in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Automatic scaling is a scale-out option that automatically handles scaling decisions for your web apps and App Service plans. It's different from Azure autoscale, which lets you define scaling rules based on metrics and schedules.
notes.example: Like a shop that opens more tills as the queue grows, with no staffing rota written in advance.

notes.front: In App Service automatic scaling, what are prewarmed instances?
notes.back: Instances kept already warmed as a buffer during scale-out and activation events.
notes.explanation: The buffer is kept until the maximum scale-out limit is reached.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Automatic scaling in Azure App Service”, “Update prewarmed instances” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The prewarmed instance setting provides warmed instances as a buffer during HTTP scale and activation events. Prewarmed instances continue to buffer until the maximum scale-out limit is reached.
notes.example: Like a spare till already switched on, ready for the next customer.

notes.front: What is the free App Service managed certificate?
notes.back: A free server certificate for your custom domain that App Service creates, manages and renews automatically.
notes.explanation: You create and bind it to a custom domain, and App Service does the rest.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Add and manage TLS/SSL certificates in Azure App Service”, “Create a free managed certificate” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The free App Service managed certificate is a turn-key solution for helping to secure your custom DNS name in App Service. Without any action from you, this TLS server certificate is fully managed by App Service and is automatically renewed, as long as the prerequisites that you set up stay the same.
notes.example: Like a door lock the landlord fits and replaces for you, at no charge.

notes.front: What are App Service access restrictions?
notes.back: Firewall-like rules that block and filter inbound traffic to an app.
notes.explanation: They cover inbound access only, not calls the app makes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure App Service access restrictions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Access restrictions in App Service are equivalent to a firewall allowing you to block and filter traffic. Access restrictions apply to **inbound** access only.
notes.example: Like a guest list checked at the front door of the app.

notes.front: What is App Service virtual network integration?
notes.back: A feature that lets an app make outbound requests into an Azure virtual network.
notes.explanation: It places the back end of the app in a subnet of a virtual network in the same region.
notes.source: Microsoft, “App Service networking features”, “Virtual network integration” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: App Service virtual network integration enables your app to make *outbound* requests into an Azure virtual network.
notes.example: Like giving the app a desk inside the private office network, so it can reach the database there.

notes.front: What is a private endpoint for an App Service app?
notes.back: A network interface with a private address from your virtual network that connects privately to the app, for inbound traffic only.
notes.explanation: It effectively brings the web app into your virtual network.
notes.source: Microsoft, “App Service networking features”, “Private endpoint” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Private endpoint is a network interface that connects you privately and securely to your Web App by Azure private link. Private endpoint uses a private IP address from your virtual network, effectively bringing the web app into your virtual network. This feature is only for *inbound* flows to your web app.
notes.example: Like a private side door into the app that opens only from the office network.

notes.front: What are App Service Hybrid Connections?
notes.back: An App Service feature for outbound calls to specific `TCP` endpoints, on-premises or anywhere that allows outbound traffic to Azure on port 443.
notes.explanation: A relay agent called Hybrid Connection Manager carries the traffic.
notes.source: Microsoft, “App Service networking features”, “Hybrid Connections” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: App Service Hybrid Connections enables your apps to make *outbound* calls to specified TCP endpoints. The endpoint can be on-premises, in a virtual network, or anywhere that allows outbound traffic to Azure on port 443.
notes.example: Like one phone extension from the app to a single server in your own building.

notes.front: In App Service, what is a deployment slot?
notes.back: A separate live app, with its own host name, that you deploy to instead of the default production slot.
notes.explanation: App content and configuration can be swapped between two slots, including production.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up staging environments in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: you can use a separate deployment slot instead of the default production slot. This approach is available if you run in the Standard, Premium, or Isolated tier of an App Service plan. Deployment slots are live apps with their own host names.
notes.example: Like a rehearsal stage beside the main stage, where the show is checked before it moves across.

notes.front: What is a deployment slot setting?
notes.back: An app setting or connection string marked as slot-specific, so it isn't swapped with the app.
notes.explanation: The setting stays with its slot when the app content moves.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up staging environments in Azure App Service”, “Make an app setting unswappable” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Add or edit a setting, and then select **Deployment slot setting**. Selecting this checkbox tells App Service that the setting isn't swappable.
notes.example: Like a name plate that stays on the office door when its occupant moves to another office.

notes.front: What is swap with preview?
notes.back: A multi-phase swap that pauses after the first step, so you can check the source slot with the target's settings before completing.
notes.explanation: It suits mission-critical apps, where you want to validate before swapping into production.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up staging environments in Azure App Service”, “Swap with preview (multiple-phase swap)” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you perform a swap with preview, App Service performs the same swap operation but pauses after the first step. You can then verify the result on the staging slot before completing the swap.
notes.example: Like a dress rehearsal in full costume before the curtain goes up.

notes.front: What is auto swap in App Service?
notes.back: A slot setting that swaps the app into its target slot automatically, after warm-up, each time you push code to the source slot.
notes.explanation: It streamlines continuous deployment with zero cold starts and zero downtime.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up staging environments in Azure App Service”, “Configure auto swap” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When auto swap is enabled from a slot into production, every time you push your code changes to that slot, App Service automatically swaps the app into production after it's warmed up in the source slot.
notes.example: Like a conveyor that moves each finished item onto the shop floor without a manual check.

notes.front: What are three things an App Service plan defines?
notes.back: Any three of: operating system, region, number of virtual machine instances, instance size, pricing tier.
notes.explanation: The pricing tier is also part of the plan.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure App Service plans?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Each App Service plan defines: - Operating system (Windows, Linux) - Region (West US, East US, and so on) - Number of virtual machine (VM) instances - Size of VM instances (small, medium, large)

notes.front: Which App Service tier category runs apps on the same virtual machine as other customers' apps?
notes.back: Shared compute: the Free and Shared tiers.
notes.explanation: Each app gets a processor quota rather than dedicated machines.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure App Service plans?”, “Pricing tiers” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Free and Shared, the two base tiers, run an app on the same Azure VM as other App Service apps, including apps of other customers. These tiers allocate CPU quotas to each app that you run.

notes.front: Which App Service tier category runs apps on dedicated virtual machines shared only by apps in the same plan?
notes.back: Dedicated compute: Basic, Standard, Premium, PremiumV2, PremiumV3 and PremiumV4.
notes.explanation: Compute is dedicated at the plan level, not per app.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure App Service plans?”, “Pricing tiers” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Basic, Standard, Premium, PremiumV2, PremiumV3, and PremiumV4 tiers run apps on dedicated Azure VMs. Only apps in the same App Service plan share the same VM instances.

notes.front: Which App Service tier adds network isolation on top of compute isolation?
notes.back: IsolatedV2, which runs dedicated virtual machines on dedicated Azure virtual networks.
notes.explanation: It also isolates your apps from other customers.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure App Service plans?”, “Pricing tiers” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The IsolatedV2 tier runs dedicated Azure VMs on dedicated Azure virtual networks. This tier provides network isolation on top of compute isolation to your apps.

notes.front: In the Free and Shared tiers, can an app scale out?
notes.back: No. It gets processor minutes on a shared virtual machine instance and can't scale out.
notes.explanation: Scaling out needs a dedicated tier.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure App Service plans?”, “Considerations for running and scaling an app” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In the Free and Shared tiers, an app receives CPU minutes on a shared VM instance and can't scale out.

notes.front: Several apps and their deployment slots sit in one Standard App Service plan. Which virtual machine instances do they run on?
notes.back: All of them share the same virtual machine instances of the plan.
notes.explanation: This is the default behaviour when per-app scaling is disabled.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure App Service plans?”, “Considerations for running and scaling an app” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If multiple apps are in the same App Service plan, they all share the same VM instances. - If you have multiple deployment slots for an app, all deployment slots also run on the same VM instances.

notes.front: In the dedicated compute tiers, what exactly is charged?
notes.back: Each virtual machine instance that the plan defines.
notes.explanation: In the Shared tier, by contrast, each app is charged for its processor quota.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure App Service plans?”, “Cost of App Service plans” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Dedicated compute tiers (Basic, Standard, Premium, PremiumV2, PremiumV3, PremiumV4)**: The App Service plan defines the number of VM instances that the apps are scaled to, so *each VM instance* is charged.

notes.front: Does an App Service plan with no apps still incur charges?
notes.back: Yes: it keeps reserving its configured virtual machine instances.
notes.explanation: To keep such a plan without paying, change it to the Free tier.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manage an App Service plan in Azure”, “Delete an App Service plan” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: App Service plans that have no apps associated with them still incur charges because they continue to reserve the configured VM instances.

notes.front: What are two reasons to isolate an app in a new App Service plan?
notes.back: Any two of: the app is resource-intensive, it must scale independently, it needs resources in another region.
notes.explanation: Putting apps together can save money, but only if the plan has enough resources for them all.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure App Service plans?”, “Decision to use a new plan or an existing plan for an app” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You want to scale the app independently from the other apps in the existing plan. - The app needs resources in a different geographical region.

notes.front: When creating an App Service plan, what do you choose in the App Service Plan details section?
notes.back: A name, the operating system and the region.
notes.explanation: Pricing tier and zone redundancy are chosen in later sections.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manage an App Service plan in Azure”, “Create an App Service plan” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In the **App Service Plan details** section, name the App Service plan, and then select the **Operating System** and **Region**. The region specifies where your App Service plan is created.

notes.front: What must be true of two App Service plans before you can move an app between them?
notes.back: Same resource group, same geographical region and same operating system type.
notes.explanation: A change such as Windows to Linux isn't supported.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manage an App Service plan in Azure”, “Move an app to another App Service plan” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can move an app to another App Service plan, as long as the source plan and the target plan are in the same resource group and geographical region and of the same OS type.

notes.front: How do you scale an App Service plan up or down?
notes.back: By changing the plan's pricing tier, which you can do at any time.
notes.explanation: You can start on a low tier and move up when you need more features.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure App Service plans?”, “Scaling for capabilities or features” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can scale your App Service plan up or down at any time. It's as simple as changing the pricing tier of the plan.

notes.front: To how many instances can a Basic App Service plan scale out?
notes.back: As many as 3.
notes.explanation: Standard reaches 10 and Premium 30.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Scale up an app in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Basic, Standard, and Premium service plans scale out to as many as 3, 10, and 30 instances, respectively.

notes.front: To how many instances can a Standard App Service plan scale out?
notes.back: As many as 10.
notes.explanation: Basic reaches only 3.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Scale up an app in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Basic, Standard, and Premium service plans scale out to as many as 3, 10, and 30 instances, respectively.

notes.front: To how many instances can a Premium App Service plan scale out?
notes.back: As many as 30.
notes.explanation: App Service Environments in the Isolated tier go further, to 100.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Scale up an app in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Basic, Standard, and Premium service plans scale out to as many as 3, 10, and 30 instances, respectively.

notes.front: Do App Service scale settings require you to change code or redeploy?
notes.back: No. They apply in seconds and affect all apps in the plan.
notes.explanation: Every app in the plan is affected because they share its instances.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Scale up an app in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The scale settings take only seconds to apply and affect all apps in your App Service plan. They don't require you to change your code or redeploy your application.

notes.front: In the portal, where do you scale up an app's pricing tier?
notes.back: On the app's page, under App Service plan, select Scale up.
notes.explanation: You then pick one of the pricing tiers and confirm with Select.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Scale up an app in Azure App Service”, “Scale up your pricing tier” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In the left pane of your App Service app page, under **App Service plan**, select **Scale up**.

notes.front: Which App Service tiers support automatic scaling?
notes.back: Premium v2 to v4.
notes.explanation: Manual scaling is available from Basic and autoscale from Standard.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Automatic scaling in Azure App Service”, “Scale-out options available in App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Available tiers | Basic and up | Standard and up | Premium v2 - v4 |

notes.front: From which App Service tier is rule-based Azure autoscale available?
notes.back: Standard and up.
notes.explanation: Manual scale-out starts at Basic.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Automatic scaling in Azure App Service”, “Scale-out options available in App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Available tiers | Basic and up | Standard and up | Premium v2 - v4 |

notes.front: How many scaling methods should be active for one App Service plan?
notes.back: Only one.
notes.explanation: Pick automatic scaling or autoscale, not both.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Automatic scaling in Azure App Service”, “Before you begin” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you need CPU-, memory-, or time-based scaling, use autoscale instead. Only one scaling method should be active for an App Service plan.

notes.front: In automatic scaling, what does the Maximum burst setting set?
notes.back: The highest number of instances the App Service plan can grow to under incoming load; up to 30 on Premium v2 to v4.
notes.explanation: It must be at least the number of workers set for the plan.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Automatic scaling in Azure App Service”, “Enable automatic scaling” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The **Maximum burst** setting represents the highest number of instances that your App Service plan can increase to based on incoming HTTP requests. For Premium v2, v3, and v4 plans, you can specify up to 30 instances.

notes.front: Which automatic scaling setting gives a web app its minimum number of instances?
notes.back: Always ready instances.
notes.explanation: Above that minimum, instances are added up to the plan's Maximum burst.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Automatic scaling in Azure App Service”, “Set the minimum number of web app instances” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The app-level setting **Always ready instances** specifies the minimum number of instances.

notes.front: Which automatic scaling setting caps how many instances one web app can scale to?
notes.back: Maximum scale limit, set between 1 and the Maximum burst value.
notes.explanation: It helps when a downstream component, such as a database, has limited throughput.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Automatic scaling in Azure App Service”, “Set the maximum number of web app instances” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The **Maximum scale limit** value sets the maximum number of instances a web app can scale to. The **Maximum scale limit** is helpful when a downstream component like a database has limited throughput.

notes.front: What is the default number of prewarmed instances, and where can you change it?
notes.back: 1; it can be changed with the Azure CLI, not in the portal.
notes.explanation: The source advises leaving it at 1 for most scenarios.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Automatic scaling in Azure App Service”, “Update prewarmed instances” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The default prewarmed instance count is *1* and, for most scenarios, this value should remain as 1.

notes.front: How are instances billed under App Service automatic scaling?
notes.back: Per second, for every instance, prewarmed instances included.
notes.explanation: Prewarmed instances act as a buffer for smooth scaling.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Automatic scaling in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You're billed per second for every instance, including prewarmed instances.

notes.front: In the portal, how do you start creating a web app?
notes.back: Search for App Services, then on the App Services page select Create > Web App.
notes.explanation: The Basics tab then asks for resource group, name, publish type, runtime stack, operating system, region and plan.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Quickstart: Deploy an ASP.NET web app”, “Publish your web app” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In the **App Services** page, select **Create** > **Web App**.

notes.front: Which App Service plan tiers let you add certificates to an app?
notes.back: Basic, Standard, Premium or Isolated.
notes.explanation: An app in a lower tier must be scaled up first.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Add and manage TLS/SSL certificates in Azure App Service”, “Prerequisites” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The app's [App Service plan](overview-hosting-plans.md) must be in the Basic, Standard, Premium, or Isolated tier.

notes.front: Which certificate option lets Azure manage a private certificate while keeping renewal and export options?
notes.back: Importing an App Service certificate.
notes.explanation: You buy and configure the App Service certificate first, then import it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Add and manage TLS/SSL certificates in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure manages the private certificate. It combines the simplicity of automated certificate management and the flexibility of renewal and export options.

notes.front: When is importing a certificate from Azure Key Vault the useful option?
notes.back: When you already manage your certificates in Key Vault.
notes.explanation: The certificate must still meet App Service's private certificate requirements.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Add and manage TLS/SSL certificates in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Import a certificate from Azure Key Vault | Useful if you use Key Vault to manage your PKCS12 certificates.

notes.front: You already hold a private certificate from a non-Microsoft provider. Which option adds it to App Service?
notes.back: Upload a private certificate.
notes.explanation: It must meet the private certificate requirements.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Add and manage TLS/SSL certificates in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you already have a private certificate from a non-Microsoft provider, you can upload it.

notes.front: For a free managed certificate on a root domain, why must the app have no IP restrictions?
notes.back: Creating and periodically renewing the certificate depend on the app being reachable from the internet.
notes.explanation: The domain must also be mapped to App Service first.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Add and manage TLS/SSL certificates in Azure App Service”, “Prerequisites” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For a root domain (like contoso.com), make sure that your app doesn't have any [IP restrictions](app-service-ip-restrictions.md) configured. Both certificate creation and its periodic renewal for a root domain depend on your app being reachable from the internet.

notes.front: Does the free App Service managed certificate support wildcard certificates?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: It also isn't exportable and doesn't support private DNS.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Add and manage TLS/SSL certificates in Azure App Service”, “Create a free managed certificate” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The free certificate comes with the following limitations: - Doesn't support wildcard certificates.

notes.front: After adding a certificate to an app, what must you still create to secure a custom domain with it?
notes.back: A certificate binding.
notes.explanation: Adding the certificate to the app does not by itself secure the domain.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Add and manage TLS/SSL certificates in Azure App Service”, “Create a free managed certificate” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To provide security for a custom domain with this certificate, you must create a certificate binding.

notes.front: Before importing a certificate from Key Vault, what access must you grant?
notes.back: Read access for the App Service resource provider to the key vault.
notes.explanation: You can grant it with an access policy or with role-based access control.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Add and manage TLS/SSL certificates in Azure App Service”, “Import a certificate from Key Vault” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By default, the App Service resource provider doesn't have access to your key vault. To use a key vault for a certificate deployment, you must authorize read access for the resource provider (App Service) to the key vault.

notes.front: Which binding type, `SNI SSL` or `IP based SSL`, lets several certificates secure several domains on the same address?
notes.back: `SNI SSL`: you can add multiple such bindings.
notes.explanation: Most modern browsers support Server Name Indication.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Enable HTTPS for a custom domain in Azure App Service”, “Add the binding” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can add multiple Server Name Indication (SNI) Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) bindings. This option allows multiple Transport Layer Security (TLS)/SSL certificates to help secure multiple domains on the same IP address.

notes.front: How many `IP based SSL` bindings can an app have, and which tier does it need?
notes.back: Only one, securing a dedicated public address; Standard tier or higher.
notes.explanation: After binding it, you remap records to the new dedicated address.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Enable HTTPS for a custom domain in Azure App Service”, “Add the binding” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can add only one IP SSL binding. This option allows only one TLS/SSL certificate to help secure a dedicated public IP address.

notes.front: Which Transport Layer Security version does an App Service app allow by default?
notes.back: Version 1.2.
notes.explanation: Industry standards such as the payment card standard recommend this level; other versions are set in general settings.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Enable HTTPS for a custom domain in Azure App Service”, “How can I change the minimum TLS versions for the app?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Your app allows [TLS](https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_Layer_Security) 1.2 by default. Industry standards such as [PCI DSS](https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Payment_Card_Industry_Data_Security_Standard) recommend this TLS level.

notes.front: Which domain record type is recommended to map a root domain such as contoso.com to App Service?
notes.back: An `A` record; don't use a `CNAME` for the root domain.
notes.explanation: The docs rule out a `CNAME` at the root domain, citing an internet standard for domain names, so the root maps straight to the app's IP address with an `A` record.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up an existing custom domain in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Root domain | `contoso.com` | [A record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_DNS_record_types#A). Don't use the CNAME record for the root domain.

notes.front: Which domain record type is recommended to map a subdomain such as www.contoso.com, and why?
notes.back: A `CNAME` record: it maps to the app's default host name, which is less likely to change than its address.
notes.explanation: An `A` record works too, but the app's address can change.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up an existing custom domain in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The CNAME maps to the app's default hostname instead, which is less susceptible to change.

notes.front: Besides the mapping record, which record does App Service use to verify you own a custom domain?
notes.back: A `TXT` record named `asuid` (or `asuid.<subdomain>`) holding the domain verification ID.
notes.explanation: The verification ID helps prevent subdomain takeovers by other App Service apps.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up an existing custom domain in Azure App Service”, “Create the DNS records” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For the root domain, App Service accesses the `asuid` TXT record to verify your ownership of the custom domain.

notes.front: Which App Service plan tier can't use a custom domain?
notes.back: The Free tier: the plan must be a paid tier.
notes.explanation: To use one, scale the plan up.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up an existing custom domain in Azure App Service”, “Prerequisites” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The web app's [App Service plan](overview-hosting-plans.md) must be a paid tier, not the Free (F1) tier.

notes.front: In the portal, where do you start mapping a custom domain to an app?
notes.back: Under Settings, select Custom domains, then Add custom domain.
notes.explanation: You then choose the provider, certificate, domain and record type, and validate.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up an existing custom domain in Azure App Service”, “Configure a custom domain” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In the sidebar menu for your app, under **Settings**, select **Custom domains**. 1. Select **Add custom domain**.

notes.front: Which App Service tiers support back up and restore, and what is the limit in Basic?
notes.back: Basic, Standard, Premium and Isolated; Basic can back up and restore only the production slot.
notes.explanation: Free and Shared are not in the list.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Back up and restore your app in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Back up and restore is supported in the Basic, Standard, Premium, and Isolated tiers. For the Basic tier, you can only back up and restore the production slot.

notes.front: How often are automatic App Service backups taken, and how long are they kept?
notes.back: Hourly, kept for 30 days; neither can be configured.
notes.explanation: Older automatic backups are thinned: every third hourly backup is kept from day 4, every sixth from day 15.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Back up and restore your app in Azure App Service”, “Automatic vs. custom backups” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Hourly, not configurable. | Configurable (every 2 hours minimum, up to 12 backups per day (manual + scheduled)). | | Retention | 30 days, not configurable.

notes.front: What do custom App Service backups need that automatic ones don't?
notes.back: A storage account, and initial configuration.
notes.explanation: The storage account must support shared access signature authorisation.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Back up and restore your app in Azure App Service”, “Automatic vs. custom backups” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: [Storage account](../storage/index.yml) required | No. | Yes. | | Backup frequency | Hourly, not configurable.

notes.front: What kind of storage account authorisation do custom App Service backups need?
notes.back: Shared access signature (SAS) authorisation; managed identity isn't supported.
notes.explanation: The storage account is chosen when you configure custom backups.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Back up and restore your app in Azure App Service”, “Create a custom backup” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Custom backups for Azure App Service require an Azure Storage account that supports Shared Access Signature (SAS)–based authorization. Managed Identity–based authentication to the storage account isn't supported for App Service backup and restore operations.

notes.front: In the portal, how do you set up custom backups?
notes.back: Backups > Configure custom backups: choose a storage account and container, then Configure.
notes.explanation: After that you can run Backup Now at any time.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Back up and restore your app in Azure App Service”, “Create a custom backup” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: At the top of the **Backups** page, select **Configure custom backups**.

notes.front: What happens to the target app while App Service restores a backup into it?
notes.back: App Service stops the target app or slot.
notes.explanation: Restoring to a slot and swapping avoids that downtime in production.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Back up and restore your app in Azure App Service”, “Restore a backup” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: App Service stops the target app or target slot while restoring a backup. To minimize downtime for a production app, restore the backup to a deployment slot first, and then swap into production.

notes.front: From what date will App Service custom backups stop backing up linked databases?
notes.back: 31 March 2028.
notes.explanation: The source recommends each database service's native backup tools instead.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Back up and restore your app in Azure App Service”, “Deprecation of linked database backups” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Starting **3/31/2028**, Azure App Service custom backups will **no longer support backing up linked databases**.

notes.front: By default, how reachable is an app hosted in App Service, and what can it reach?
notes.back: It is reachable directly from the internet and can reach only internet-hosted endpoints.
notes.explanation: Networking features control the inbound and outbound traffic beyond this default.
notes.source: Microsoft, “App Service networking features” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By default, apps hosted in App Service are accessible directly through the internet and can reach only internet-hosted endpoints.

notes.front: Do access restrictions apply to traffic that arrives through a private endpoint?
notes.back: No. Private endpoint traffic goes directly to the site without these restrictions.
notes.explanation: Private endpoint traffic is restricted with network security groups instead.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure App Service access restrictions”, “How it works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If the traffic is sent through a private endpoint, it sends directly to the site without any restrictions. Restrictions to private endpoints are configured using network security groups.

notes.front: In what order are access restriction rules evaluated?
notes.back: In priority order.
notes.explanation: Rules with the same priority are evaluated in the order they are listed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure App Service access restrictions”, “How it works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Access restriction rules are evaluated in priority order.

notes.front: If you haven't configured the unmatched rule, what happens to traffic that matches no access restriction rule?
notes.back: With no rules, all access is allowed; once one or more rules exist, unmatched traffic is denied.
notes.explanation: You can set the unmatched behaviour explicitly to allow or deny.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure App Service access restrictions”, “Unmatched rule” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If there are no rules, the unmatched rule behavior is to allow all access, but if one or more rules exists it implicitly changes to deny all access.

notes.front: Does virtual network integration give resources in the virtual network private inbound access to the app?
notes.back: No. It is used only for outbound calls from the app; inbound private access needs a private endpoint.
notes.explanation: Private endpoints handle inbound private access.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Integrate your app with an Azure virtual network” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Virtual network integration gives your app access to resources in your virtual network, but it doesn't grant inbound private access to your app from the virtual network.

notes.front: Can an app in the Free or Shared tier use virtual network integration?
notes.back: No. It needs Basic, Standard, Premium v1 to v4, or Elastic Premium.
notes.explanation: It supports `TCP` and `UDP` and works with App Service, function and Logic apps.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Integrate your app with an Azure virtual network” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Requires a Basic, Standard, Premium, Premium v2, Premium v3, Premium v4, or Elastic Premium App Service pricing tier.

notes.front: Why size a virtual network integration subnet generously from the start?
notes.back: Its size can't be changed after assignment.
notes.explanation: The source recommends double the addresses of your planned maximum scale; a /26 covers one multitenant plan's maximum.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Integrate your app with an Azure virtual network”, “Subnet requirements” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Because subnet size can't be changed after assignment, use a subnet that's large enough to accommodate whatever scale your app might reach.

notes.front: What can be reached across an app's private endpoint?
notes.back: Only the app it is configured for, which prevents data exfiltration.
notes.explanation: It is for inbound flows only.
notes.source: Microsoft, “App Service networking features”, “Private endpoint” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Private endpoints prevent data exfiltration. The only thing you can reach across the private endpoint is the app with which it's configured.

notes.front: What must you install to use App Service Hybrid Connections, and where?
notes.back: The Hybrid Connection Manager relay agent, on a Windows Server 2012 or newer host that can reach Azure Relay on port 443.
notes.explanation: You download it from the Hybrid Connections page in the portal.
notes.source: Microsoft, “App Service networking features”, “Hybrid Connections” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To use the feature, you need to install a relay agent called Hybrid Connection Manager on a Windows Server 2012 or newer host. Hybrid Connection Manager needs to be able to reach Azure Relay at port 443.

notes.front: Which App Service tiers support deployment slots?
notes.back: Standard, Premium and Isolated.
notes.explanation: In the portal, an app on a lower tier shows an Upgrade option instead.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up staging environments in Azure App Service”, “Add a slot” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For you to enable multiple deployment slots, the app must be running in the Standard, Premium, or Isolated tier.

notes.front: How many deployment slots does the Standard tier support?
notes.back: Five.
notes.explanation: Each tier supports a different number of slots.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up staging environments in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For example, if your app has more than five slots, you can't scale it down to the Standard tier. The Standard tier supports only five deployment slots.

notes.front: You add a slot and clone settings from production. What content does the new slot have?
notes.back: None: a new slot has no content, even with cloned settings.
notes.explanation: You then deploy to it, for example from another branch.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up staging environments in Azure App Service”, “Add a slot” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The new deployment slot has no content, even if you clone the settings from a different slot.

notes.front: In the portal, where do you add a deployment slot?
notes.back: Deployment > Deployment slots, then Add.
notes.explanation: You name the slot and may clone configuration from another slot.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up staging environments in Azure App Service”, “Add a slot” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: On the left menu, select **Deployment** > **Deployment slots**. Then select **Add**.

notes.front: In the first step of a swap, what does App Service apply to the source slot's instances?
notes.back: The target slot's slot-specific settings, plus its continuous deployment and authentication settings if enabled.
notes.explanation: Applying them restarts every instance in the source slot.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up staging environments in Azure App Service”, “Swap operation steps” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Apply the following settings from the target slot (for example, the production slot) to all instances of the source slot: - [Slot-specific](#which-settings-are-swapped) app settings and connection strings, if applicable - [Continuous deployment](deploy-continuous-deployment.md) settings, if enabled - [App Service authentication](overview-authentication-authorization.md) settings, if enabled

notes.front: Where do you mark an app setting as a deployment slot setting in the portal?
notes.back: In the slot's Settings > Environment Variable: edit the setting, tick Deployment slot setting, then Apply.
notes.explanation: Connection strings can be made slot-specific in the same way.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up staging environments in Azure App Service”, “Make an app setting unswappable” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Go to **Settings** > **Environment Variable** for that slot. 1. Add or edit a setting, and then select **Deployment slot setting**.

notes.front: How do you roll back a swap that caused errors in production?
notes.back: Swap the same two slots again immediately.
notes.explanation: After a swap, the staging slot holds the previous production app.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up staging environments in Azure App Service”, “Roll back a swap” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If any errors occur in the target slot (for example, the production slot) after a slot swap, restore the slots to their pre-swap states by swapping the same two slots immediately.

notes.front: An app in a Free tier plan needs three instances at busy times. What must you do first?
notes.back: Scale the plan up to a dedicated tier such as Basic; Free can't scale out.
notes.choices:
A) Set the instance count to 3 in Free
B) Scale the plan up to Basic or higher
C) Move the app to the Shared tier
D) Add two deployment slots
notes.choicesExplained: A: Free can't scale out. C: Shared can't scale out either. D: slots are separate apps, not extra instances.
notes.explanation: Scale out only becomes possible once the plan is on a dedicated tier.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure App Service plans?”, “Considerations for running and scaling an app” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In the Free and Shared tiers, an app receives CPU minutes on a shared VM instance and can't scale out.

notes.front: Three web apps share one Standard App Service plan configured with two instances, and per-app scaling is off. On how many instances does each app run?
notes.back: Two: every app runs on all the plan's virtual machine instances.
notes.choices:
A) One each, three in total
B) Two each, shared
C) Six in total
D) Only the first app runs on both
notes.choicesExplained: A and C assume each app gets its own instances. D: all apps run on every instance by default.
notes.explanation: Adding apps to a plan adds load to the same instances, not new ones.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure App Service plans?”, “Considerations for running and scaling an app” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When the app runs, it runs on all the VM instances configured in the App Service plan. - If multiple apps are in the same App Service plan, they all share the same VM instances.

notes.front: You want to move a Linux web app into a Windows App Service plan in the same resource group and region. Is this allowed?
notes.back: No. The plans must be of the same operating system type.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if both plans are Standard
B) No: the operating system type must match
C) Yes, after disabling virtual network integration
D) Yes, with Change plan
notes.choicesExplained: A: the tier doesn't lift the rule. C is a separate requirement, not a fix for the type mismatch. D is the portal step, but the move itself isn't supported.
notes.explanation: Resource group and region match, but the operating system type doesn't.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manage an App Service plan in Azure”, “Move an app to another App Service plan” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Any change in type, such as Windows to Linux or any type that's different from the originating type, isn't supported.

notes.front: Regulations require an app's compute to be isolated from other customers and to run in its own dedicated virtual network. Which tier fits?
notes.back: IsolatedV2.
notes.choices:
A) Shared
B) Standard
C) PremiumV3
D) IsolatedV2
notes.choicesExplained: A shares virtual machines with other customers. B and C are dedicated compute, but not on a dedicated virtual network.
notes.explanation: Only the isolated category adds network isolation on top of compute isolation.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure App Service plans?”, “Pricing tiers” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The IsolatedV2 tier runs dedicated Azure VMs on dedicated Azure virtual networks. This tier provides network isolation on top of compute isolation to your apps.

notes.front: You delete the only app in a plan but keep the plan for later. How do you avoid paying for it meanwhile?
notes.back: Change the plan to the Free tier.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: empty plans are free
B) Change the plan to the Free tier
C) Stop the plan
D) Scale out to zero instances
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: empty plans still incur charges. C and D are not the step the source gives.
notes.explanation: An empty plan still reserves, and pays for, its configured instances.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manage an App Service plan in Azure”, “Delete an App Service plan” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you choose to keep the plan, you should change the plan to the **Free** tier so that you're not charged.

notes.front: An app needs custom domains and staging slots it doesn't have today. Is that a scale-up or a scale-out change?
notes.back: Scale up: change the plan's pricing tier.
notes.choices:
A) Scale up
B) Scale out
C) Automatic scaling
D) Per-app scaling
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D change instance counts, not the features available.
notes.explanation: Features come with the tier; scale out only adds instances.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Scale up an app in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Scale up: Get more CPU, memory, or disk space, or extra features like dedicated virtual machines (VMs), custom domains and certificates, staging slots, or autoscaling. You scale up by changing the pricing tier of the App Service plan that your app belongs to.

notes.front: A Standard plan runs at 10 instances and still needs more. What is the next step?
notes.back: Scale up to Premium, which scales out to as many as 30 instances.
notes.choices:
A) Scale out to 15 in Standard
B) Scale up to Premium
C) Scale down to Basic
D) Enable Hybrid Connections
notes.choicesExplained: A exceeds Standard's limit of 10. C lowers the limit to 3. D is a networking feature.
notes.explanation: Standard's limit is 10, so more instances need a higher tier.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Scale up an app in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Basic, Standard, and Premium service plans scale out to as many as 3, 10, and 30 instances, respectively.

notes.front: A web app must scale on a timetable, adding instances every weekday morning. Automatic scaling or Azure autoscale?
notes.back: Azure autoscale.
notes.choices:
A) App Service automatic scaling
B) Azure autoscale
C) Manual scaling
D) Prewarmed instances
notes.choicesExplained: A has no schedule-based scaling. C needs someone to act each morning. D is a buffer setting within automatic scaling.
notes.explanation: Automatic scaling reacts to web traffic only and has no schedules.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Automatic scaling in Azure App Service”, “Before you begin” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Autoscale:** - Uses metrics (CPU, memory, queue length, custom metrics) - Supports schedule-based scaling - Applies to the entire App Service plan

notes.front: Two web apps in one Premium v3 plan should scale on their own web traffic, independently, with no rules to maintain. Which option fits?
notes.back: App Service automatic scaling.
notes.choices:
A) Azure autoscale
B) App Service automatic scaling
C) Manual scaling
D) Scale up to IsolatedV2
notes.choicesExplained: A applies to the whole plan and uses rules. C is not automatic. D changes the tier, not how apps scale.
notes.explanation: Automatic scaling is configured per app and needs no rules.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Automatic scaling in Azure App Service”, “How automatic scaling works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You want your web apps within the same App Service plan to scale differently and independently of each other.

notes.front: An app with automatic scaling has 3 always-ready instances, the default prewarmed setting, and no traffic yet. Is a prewarmed instance being billed?
notes.back: No. A prewarmed instance is allocated, and billed, only once the always-ready instances become active.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, always
B) No, not until the app receives requests
C) Yes, three of them
D) No, prewarmed instances are never billed
notes.choicesExplained: A and C ignore that none is allocated while idle. D is wrong: prewarmed instances are billed per second once allocated.
notes.explanation: Billing for the prewarmed instance starts when requests arrive.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Automatic scaling in Azure App Service”, “How do I get billed for prewarmed instances?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When your web app is idle and not receiving any HTTP requests, it runs with the five always-ready instances. During this time, you aren't billed for a prewarmed instance because the always-ready instances aren't being used, and thus no prewarmed instance is allocated.

notes.front: On the Create Web App Basics tab, you must deploy code rather than a container, on a specific language version. Which two settings express this?
notes.back: Publish: Code, and the Runtime stack.
notes.choices:
A) Publish and Runtime stack
B) Region and Name
C) Pricing plan and Region
D) Resource group and Name
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D don't describe how or in what language the app is deployed.
notes.explanation: The other Basics settings name, place and size the app rather than describe its code.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Quickstart: Deploy an ASP.NET web app”, “Publish your web app” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Under **Publish**, select *Code*. - Under **Runtime stack** select *.NET 8 (LTS)*.

notes.front: You want to add a certificate to an app in a Free tier plan. What must you do first?
notes.back: Scale the plan up to Basic, Standard, Premium or Isolated.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing
B) Scale the plan up to Basic or higher
C) Buy an App Service domain
D) Add a deployment slot
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the tier requirement. C gives a domain, not the tier. D needs Standard anyway and doesn't help.
notes.explanation: Certificates can't be added in the Free tier.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Add and manage TLS/SSL certificates in Azure App Service”, “Prerequisites” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The app's [App Service plan](overview-hosting-plans.md) must be in the Basic, Standard, Premium, or Isolated tier.

notes.front: You need one certificate covering *.contoso.com on App Service. Can the free managed certificate do it?
notes.back: No. It doesn't support wildcard certificates; use another option, such as uploading your own certificate.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, it covers any subdomain
B) No: it doesn't support wildcards
C) Yes, on the Premium tier
D) Yes, if exported first
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: wildcards aren't supported on any tier. D: the free certificate isn't exportable.
notes.explanation: The free certificate covers named custom domains only.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Add and manage TLS/SSL certificates in Azure App Service”, “Create a free managed certificate” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The free certificate comes with the following limitations: - Doesn't support wildcard certificates.

notes.front: An app hosts five custom domains, each with its own certificate, and doesn't need a dedicated address. Which binding type fits?
notes.back: `SNI SSL`.
notes.choices:
A) `SNI SSL`
B) `IP based SSL`
C) No binding
D) A public certificate
notes.choicesExplained: B allows only one binding. C leaves the domains unsecured. D can't secure custom domains.
notes.explanation: `IP based SSL` allows just one binding.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Enable HTTPS for a custom domain in Azure App Service”, “Add the binding” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can add multiple Server Name Indication (SNI) Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) bindings. This option allows multiple Transport Layer Security (TLS)/SSL certificates to help secure multiple domains on the same IP address.

notes.front: An auditor asks what minimum Transport Layer Security version your new App Service app accepts if you change nothing. What do you answer?
notes.back: Version 1.2, the default.
notes.choices:
A) 1.0
B) 1.1
C) 1.2
D) None: encryption is off by default
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are older than the default. D: App Service even redirects plain requests to secure ones by default.
notes.explanation: A different minimum would need to be set in general settings.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Enable HTTPS for a custom domain in Azure App Service”, “How can I change the minimum TLS versions for the app?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Your app allows [TLS](https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_Layer_Security) 1.2 by default.

notes.front: You are mapping both contoso.com and www.contoso.com to an app. Which record types do you create for the mappings?
notes.back: An `A` record for contoso.com and a `CNAME` record for www.contoso.com.
notes.choices:
A) `CNAME` for both
B) `A` for the root, `CNAME` for www
C) `A` for both, no verification
D) `TXT` only
notes.choicesExplained: A: don't use a `CNAME` for the root domain. C skips the recommended `CNAME` and the verification record. D verifies ownership but maps nothing.
notes.explanation: Each also needs its `TXT` verification record.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up an existing custom domain in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Root domain | `contoso.com` | [A record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_DNS_record_types#A). Don't use the CNAME record for the root domain.

notes.front: Your domain's mapping record is correct, but you worry that another App Service app could take over the subdomain. What should you add?
notes.back: The `asuid` `TXT` record with the domain verification ID.
notes.choices:
A) A second `A` record
B) The `asuid` `TXT` record
C) A wildcard `CNAME`
D) Access restrictions
notes.choicesExplained: A and C map names but don't prove ownership. D filters traffic, not domain ownership.
notes.explanation: The record is not strictly required, but the source highly recommends it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up an existing custom domain in Azure App Service”, “Configure a custom domain” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: While it's not absolutely required to add the TXT record, it's highly recommended for security. The TXT record is a *domain verification ID* that helps avoid subdomain takeovers from other App Service apps.

notes.front: An app on the Free tier needs the custom domain shop.contoso.com. What must change?
notes.back: Scale the plan to a paid tier.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing
B) Scale to a paid tier
C) Use a private zone
D) Add a deployment slot
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the prerequisite. C: private zones aren't supported. D doesn't change the tier.
notes.explanation: Custom domains aren't available on Free.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up an existing custom domain in Azure App Service”, “Prerequisites” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The web app's [App Service plan](overview-hosting-plans.md) must be a paid tier, not the Free (F1) tier.

notes.front: An app on the Basic tier has a staging slot. Can you back up the staging slot?
notes.back: No. On Basic you can back up and restore only the production slot.
notes.choices:
A) Yes
B) No: Basic backs up only production
C) Yes, with automatic backups only
D) No: Basic has no backups at all
notes.choicesExplained: A and C ignore the Basic limit. D is wrong: Basic supports backups of the production slot.
notes.explanation: Backups of other slots need a higher tier.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Back up and restore your app in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For the Basic tier, you can only back up and restore the production slot.

notes.front: You need an App Service backup you can download and keep for a year. Automatic or custom backup?
notes.back: A custom backup, which is downloadable and can be kept indefinitely.
notes.choices:
A) Automatic
B) Custom
C) Either
D) Neither
notes.choicesExplained: A is kept for 30 days and isn't downloadable. C and D ignore the difference between the two.
notes.explanation: Automatic backups are kept only 30 days and can't be downloaded.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Back up and restore your app in Azure App Service”, “Automatic vs. custom backups” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence:
Retention | 30 days, not configurable.

Days 1-3: hourly backups retained.

Days 4-14: every third hourly backup retained.

Days 15-30: every sixth hourly backup retained. | 0-30 days or indefinite. |

notes.front: You must restore a production app from backup with minimal downtime. What does the source suggest?
notes.back: Restore into a deployment slot first, then swap it into production.
notes.choices:
A) Restore over production directly
B) Restore to a slot, then swap
C) Download the backup and redeploy
D) Scale out first
notes.choicesExplained: A stops the production app during the restore. C and D aren't the source's approach.
notes.explanation: Restoring straight into production stops the app during the restore.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Back up and restore your app in Azure App Service”, “Restore a backup” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To minimize downtime for a production app, restore the backup to a [deployment slot](deploy-staging-slots.md) first, and then [swap](deploy-staging-slots.md#swap-two-slots) into production.

notes.front: You configure a custom backup but the storage account allows only managed identity access. Will backups work?
notes.back: No. Custom backups need a storage account that supports shared access signature authorisation.
notes.choices:
A) Yes
B) No: shared access signature authorisation is needed
C) Yes, but only automatic backups
D) Yes, over a virtual network
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D ignore that managed identity isn't supported for backup and restore.
notes.explanation: Enable shared access signature authorisation on the account.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Back up and restore your app in Azure App Service”, “Create a custom backup” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Managed Identity–based authentication to the storage account isn't supported for App Service backup and restore operations.

notes.front: You want to allow traffic to an app only from your company's public address range. Inbound or outbound feature, and which one?
notes.back: Inbound: access restrictions.
notes.choices:
A) Access restrictions
B) Virtual network integration
C) Hybrid Connections
D) App-assigned address
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are outbound features. D gives the app a dedicated address but doesn't filter callers.
notes.explanation: Restricting who reaches the app is an inbound problem.
notes.source: Microsoft, “App Service networking features”, “Use cases and features” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Restrict access to your app from a set of well-defined addresses | Access restrictions |

notes.front: An app must call a database on a virtual machine in a virtual network in the same region. Which feature?
notes.back: Virtual network integration (outbound).
notes.choices:
A) Private endpoint
B) Access restrictions
C) Virtual network integration
D) App-assigned address
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D are inbound features.
notes.explanation: Calling out of the app is an outbound problem.
notes.source: Microsoft, “App Service networking features”, “Use cases and features” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Access resources in an Azure virtual network in the same region | Virtual network integration </br> ASE |

notes.front: An app must reach one server in a branch office that has no VPN or ExpressRoute link to Azure. Which feature fits?
notes.back: Hybrid Connections.
notes.choices:
A) Virtual network integration
B) Hybrid Connections
C) Private endpoint
D) Access restrictions
notes.choicesExplained: A needs a virtual network path. C and D are inbound features.
notes.explanation: Hybrid Connections doesn't depend on a virtual network.
notes.source: Microsoft, “App Service networking features”, “Use cases and features” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Access resources in a private network that's not connected to Azure | Hybrid Connections |

notes.front: You add one allow rule for your office range and leave the unmatched rule unset. What happens to other visitors?
notes.back: They are denied: with one or more rules, unmatched traffic is denied.
notes.choices:
A) Allowed
B) Denied
C) Redirected to the scm site
D) Queued
notes.choicesExplained: A would need the unmatched rule set to allow. C and D aren't behaviours of the unmatched rule.
notes.explanation: Before any rule existed, everyone was allowed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure App Service access restrictions”, “Unmatched rule” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If there are no rules, the unmatched rule behavior is to allow all access, but if one or more rules exists it implicitly changes to deny all access.

notes.front: Users on your virtual network must reach an app privately, with no public entry. You enabled virtual network integration. Is that enough?
notes.back: No. Integration is outbound only; add a private endpoint for inbound private access.
notes.choices:
A) Yes
B) No: add a private endpoint
C) No: add Hybrid Connections
D) Yes, with a larger subnet
notes.choicesExplained: A and D: integration never gives inbound access. C is also outbound.
notes.explanation: Inbound private access is a separate feature.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Integrate your app with an Azure virtual network” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Virtual network integration is used only to make outbound calls from your app into your virtual network. Refer to [private endpoint](./networking/private-endpoint.md) for inbound private access.

notes.front: A Shared tier app must call resources in a virtual network through virtual network integration. What must you do?
notes.back: Scale the plan up to at least Basic.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing
B) Scale up to Basic or higher
C) Add a private endpoint
D) Enable access restrictions
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the tier requirement. C and D are inbound features.
notes.explanation: Shared isn't among the supported tiers.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Integrate your app with an Azure virtual network” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Requires a Basic, Standard, Premium, Premium v2, Premium v3, Premium v4, or Elastic Premium App Service pricing tier.

notes.front: A team on the Basic tier wants a staging slot. What must change?
notes.back: Scale the plan up to Standard, Premium or Isolated.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing
B) Scale up to Standard or higher
C) Create a second Basic plan
D) Enable automatic scaling
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the tier requirement. C gives another app, not a slot. D is unrelated to slots.
notes.explanation: Basic has no deployment slots.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up staging environments in Azure App Service”, “Add a slot” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For you to enable multiple deployment slots, the app must be running in the Standard, Premium, or Isolated tier.

notes.front: You swap staging into production. Which slot should be the target, and why?
notes.back: Production, so all initialisation happens on staging and production stays online.
notes.choices:
A) Production is the target
B) Staging is the target
C) Either: it makes no difference
D) A new third slot
notes.choicesExplained: B would do the warm-up work on production. C: the direction matters. D isn't needed.
notes.explanation: The target slot stays online throughout the swap.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up staging environments in Azure App Service”, “Swap operation steps” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To swap a staging slot with the production slot, make sure that the production slot is always the target slot. This way, the swap operation doesn't affect your production app.

notes.front: Staging must keep its own database connection string when its app is swapped into production. What do you do?
notes.back: Mark the connection string as a deployment slot setting.
notes.choices:
A) Mark it as a deployment slot setting
B) Use swap with preview
C) Enable auto swap
D) Set traffic to 0%
notes.choicesExplained: B pauses the swap but still swaps the setting. C automates the swap. D affects routing, not settings.
notes.explanation: Slot-specific settings stay with their slot during a swap.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up staging environments in Azure App Service”, “Make an app setting unswappable” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Add or edit a setting, and then select **Deployment slot setting**. Selecting this checkbox tells App Service that the setting isn't swappable.

notes.front: Before a mission-critical release goes live, you want to check the staging slot running with production's settings. Which swap type?
notes.back: Swap with preview.
notes.choices:
A) Swap with preview
B) Auto swap
C) A normal swap
D) Traffic routing at 100%
notes.choicesExplained: B and C complete without a pause for checking. D sends users to staging without its production settings.
notes.explanation: It pauses after applying the target's settings so you can verify.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up staging environments in Azure App Service”, “Swap with preview (multiple-phase swap)” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Before you swap into production as the target slot, validate that the app runs with the swapped settings. The source slot is also warmed up before the swap completion, which is desirable for mission-critical applications.

notes.front: A Linux web app team wants every push to staging to go live automatically. Can they use auto swap?
notes.back: No. Auto swap isn't supported for web apps on Linux.
notes.choices:
A) Yes
B) No: not supported on Linux
C) Yes, on Premium only
D) Yes, with swap with preview
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D ignore that auto swap isn't supported for web apps on Linux.
notes.explanation: The limitation applies to Web App for Containers too.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up staging environments in Azure App Service”, “Configure auto swap” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Auto swap isn't supported in web apps on Linux and in Web App for Containers.

notes.front: You want 10% of production visitors to try the new version in staging. What do you set?
notes.back: Traffic % of the staging slot to 10, under Deployment slots.
notes.choices:
A) Traffic % on the staging slot
B) Swap with preview
C) Auto swap
D) Access restrictions
notes.choicesExplained: B and C move the whole app. D blocks traffic rather than splitting it.
notes.explanation: That share of clients is then routed at random to the slot.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up staging environments in Azure App Service”, “Route production traffic automatically” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In the **Traffic %** column of the slot that you want to route to, specify a percentage (between 0 and 100) to represent the amount of total traffic that you want to route.

notes.front: Scale up versus scale out in App Service: what does each change?
notes.back: Scale up changes the pricing tier (more resources and features); scale out adds virtual machine instances.
notes.explanation: Tier features such as slots come only with scaling up.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Scale up an app in Azure App Service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You scale up by changing the pricing tier of the App Service plan that your app belongs to. * Scale out: Increase the number of VM instances that run your app.

notes.front: App Service automatic scaling versus Azure autoscale: what does each scale on, and at what level is it configured?
notes.back: Automatic: incoming web traffic, per app, no rules. Autoscale: metrics and schedules, for the whole plan.
notes.explanation: Only one of the two should be active for a plan.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Automatic scaling in Azure App Service”, “Before you begin” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Scales automatically based on incoming HTTP traffic - Configured per app - Supports Always ready, per-app limits, Maximum burst, and prewarmed instances Autoscale:** - Uses metrics (CPU, memory, queue length, custom metrics) - Supports schedule-based scaling - Applies to the entire App Service plan

notes.front: `SNI SSL` versus `IP based SSL` bindings: how many can you add, and what address do they use?
notes.back: `SNI SSL`: many bindings on a shared address. `IP based SSL`: one binding on a dedicated public address, Standard or higher.
notes.explanation: `SNI SSL` lets multiple certificates share the same address.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Enable HTTPS for a custom domain in Azure App Service”, “Add the binding” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: IP based SSL**: You can add only one IP SSL binding. This option allows only one TLS/SSL certificate to help secure a dedicated public IP address.

notes.front: Automatic versus custom App Service backups: which needs configuration and a storage account, and which runs hourly?
notes.back: Custom needs configuration and a storage account; automatic needs neither and runs hourly.
notes.explanation: Custom backups also require initial configuration, and can be on demand or scheduled.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Back up and restore your app in Azure App Service”, “Automatic vs. custom backups” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: [Storage account](../storage/index.yml) required | No. | Yes. | | Backup frequency | Hourly, not configurable.

notes.front: Virtual network integration versus a private endpoint for an app: which direction of traffic does each handle?
notes.back: Virtual network integration: outbound from the app. Private endpoint: inbound to the app.
notes.explanation: Integration never grants inbound private access to the app, so an app that must also be reached privately needs a private endpoint for that direction.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Integrate your app with an Azure virtual network” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Virtual network integration is used only to make outbound calls from your app into your virtual network. Refer to [private endpoint](./networking/private-endpoint.md) for inbound private access.
